question.prompt: Each of two boxes contains three chips numbered \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3.\) A chip is drawn randomly from each box and the numbers on the two chips are multiplied. What is the probability that their product is even?

solutions.explanation:
The only even chip number is \(2\), so the product is even exactly when at least one drawn chip is numbered \(2\).

Write an outcome as \((a,b)\), where \(a\) is the first box's number and \(b\) is the second box's number. Each of the \(3\) choices from the first box can pair with each of the \(3\) choices from the second, giving \(9\) equally likely outcomes. The even-product outcomes are
\[
\begin{gathered}
(1,2),\ (2,1),\ (2,2),\\
(2,3),\ (3,2).
\end{gathered}
\]
These are all the pairs containing a \(2\), with each pair listed once. Thus the probability is \(\boxed{\frac59}\), choice \(\text{E}\).
solutions.title: List the successful pairs

solutions.explanation:
It is convenient to count the products that are odd and subtract them from all possible outcomes. A product is odd exactly when both factors are odd.

There are \(3\times3=9\) equally likely ordered pairs, recording the number from each separate box. Each box has two odd chips, numbered \(1\) and \(3\), so there are \(2\times2=4\) odd-product pairs. Pairing each first-box choice with each second-box choice includes every such outcome exactly once.

Every product is either odd or even, so the remaining \(9-4=5\) outcomes have even products. The required probability is
\[
\frac{9-4}{9}=\boxed{\frac59},
\]
choice \(\text{E}\).
